entries.meaning: Negative purpose: the clause names the thing the subject is acting to avoid. It covers the same ground as lest but stays inside ordinary modern American prose, and unlike lest it takes a normal indicative or modal verb rather than the subjunctive — for fear that he would find out, not for fear that he find out.
examples: She kept the receipt for fear that the store would refuse the return.
He never mentioned the offer for fear his boss would hear about it.
They moved the ceremony indoors for fear that the storm would arrive early.
Nobody said a word for fear that the wrong person was listening.
I checked the lock twice for fear of another break-in.
Parents pulled their kids out of the pool for fear that lightning was coming.
For fear that the news would leak overnight, the company briefed its staff and the press the same morning.
entries.русский: из страха, что; боясь, что — отрицательная цель: то, чего действием стараются избежать
entries.pattern: [main clause] for fear that [clause]. · For fear that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] for fear of [gerund/noun].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the clause when it is fronted, which is rare.
entries.variants: for fear (that-less), for fear of + gerund
entries.see also: lest, in case, in the hope that, so that, in order that

entries.meaning: Precautionary purpose — you do the main action now so that you are ready for a possibility. That is exactly what separates it from if: Take an umbrella in case it rains means take it regardless, while Take an umbrella if it rains means take it only once the rain has started. American English uses the present tense for the future contingency (in case it rains, never in case it will rain).
examples: Bring a jacket in case the theater is cold.
I wrote the address on my hand in case my phone died.
In case the power goes out, there are candles in the drawer.
We booked the second room in case her parents decided to come after all.
Save the confirmation email, just in case.
In case of fire, use the stairs.
entries.русский: на случай, если — предупредительная цель; не «если» (if): действие делается заранее
entries.pattern: [main clause] in case [clause]. · In case [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], just in case. · In case of [noun], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before in case in the normal order. Comma after the clause when it is fronted. The tag just in case at the end of a sentence does take a comma before it.
entries.variants: just in case, in case of + noun (prepositional)
entries.see also: for fear that, in the hope that, lest, so that

entries.meaning: The formal written twin of so that, and almost always followed by a modal — may, might, can, could, will, would, shall. Americans say so that or bare so in speech; in order that survives mainly in legal, academic, and ceremonial prose. Use in order to instead when both clauses share a subject and an infinitive will do.
examples: The records are sealed in order that the witnesses may be protected.
In order that everyone can attend, the meeting was moved to Friday afternoon.
Funds were set aside in order that the district might hire a second counselor.
The statute was amended in order that small businesses would not be penalized.
He repeated the instructions slowly in order that no one would misunderstand them.
In order that the record may be complete, the clerk will now read the motion.
entries.русский: чтобы, с тем чтобы — книжн. союз цели, обычно с модальным глаголом
entries.pattern: [main clause] in order that [clause with modal]. · In order that [clause with modal], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the clause when it is fronted.
entries.see also: so that, in order to, to the end that, that, lest

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈhoʊp ðæt/, reduced /ɪn ðə ˈhoʊp ðət/
entries.meaning: Purpose with the confidence taken out of it. So that presents the goal as reachable; in the hope that concedes it may not work, which is why it takes an ordinary indicative verb (in the hope that someone would answer) instead of the modal-heavy clause in order that demands. American English uses the plural in hopes that as freely as the singular.
examples: She left a note on the windshield in the hope that the driver would call.
They cut the price twice in hopes that somebody would bid.
In the hope that a deal could still be reached, the union delayed the strike vote.
He mailed the manuscript to twelve agents in the hope of a single reply.
The city planted two hundred maples in the hope that the block would be shaded by 2035.
We left the porch light on all night in hopes that the cat would find her way back.
He drove past the house twice in hopes of catching her at home.
entries.русский: в надежде, что — цель, в достижимости которой говорящий не уверен
entries.pattern: [main clause] in the hope that [clause]. · In the hope that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] in hopes that [clause]. · [main clause] in the hope of [gerund/noun].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the clause when it is fronted. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate, not independent.
entries.variants: in hopes that, in the hopes that, in the hope of + gerund, in hopes of + gerund
entries.see also: so that, in order that, for fear that, in case, with the aim of

entries.meaning: Negative purpose, equal to so that ... not or for fear that. It takes the present subjunctive — a bare verb with no -s (lest he be late, not lest he is late) — or should. The negation already sits inside the word, which is the classic trap: lest anyone hear means "so that nobody hears," so adding not reverses the sense. Everyday American speech uses so that ... doesn't or in case.
examples: He whispered the address lest anyone overhear.
She hid the letter lest her sister find it.
Lest we forget, the same promise was made five years ago.
The committee moved carefully lest it be accused of favoritism.
Keep the receipt lest there should be a dispute later.
I said nothing lest I make the argument worse.
entries.русский: чтобы не, дабы не — книжн., устар.; отрицание уже внутри слова, второе «не» лишнее
entries.pattern: [main clause] lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb]. · [main clause] lest [subject] should [verb]. · Lest [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the clause when it is fronted, as in the fixed phrase Lest we forget, ...
entries.see also: for fear that, in case, so that, in order that

entries.meaning: In casual American English bare so stands in for so that in the purpose sense, and the dropped that is completely standard in speech. The same two letters do at least four other jobs, which is why that comma has to work so hard: the coordinating conjunction of result, one of the FANBOYS (The bus never came, so we walked); the degree adverb of so ... that and of bare intensifying so (I'm so tired); the pro-form standing in for a whole clause (I think so, If so, call me); and the discourse opener that starts a turn in conversation (So, where were we?).
examples: Text me when you land so I know you got there.
She sat in the front row so she could hear the questions.
We left the porch light on so the sitter wouldn't have to hunt for the keyhole.
Write it on the calendar so you don't forget again.
The bus never came, so we walked the last mile.
Move the couch over so there's room for the tree.
entries.русский: чтобы — разг. замена so that; с запятой перед ним — «так что, поэтому» (результат)
entries.type: subordinating (reduced so that); also coordinating in the result sense
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of purpose; coordinate clause in the result sense
entries.pattern: [main clause] so [clause with modal]. — purpose · [independent clause], so [independent clause]. — result · [subject] [verb] so [adjective] that [clause]. — degree
entries.punctuation: One comma decides the meaning. No comma = purpose (I left early so I could beat traffic). Comma = result (I left early, so I beat traffic), which is the ordinary rule for a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses. A semicolon before result so is defensible only when both clauses are long and already full of commas; in an ordinary sentence it is wrong, and it is always wrong before purpose so.
entries.variants: so that (full form), so as to (infinitival), so ... that (degree)
entries.see also: so that, so ... that, so as to, so (coordinating)

entries.meaning: The default purpose subordinator of American English, and the one to reach for when the two clauses have different subjects. The purpose clause normally carries can, could, will, would, or may; drop the modal and the sentence tips toward the result reading. Compare in order that (formal), bare so (casual), and in order to (same subject, infinitive).
examples: Label the boxes so that the movers know which room each one goes in.
I set two alarms so that I wouldn't oversleep on the first day.
The city widened the sidewalk so that strollers and wheelchairs could pass each other.
She froze half the soup so that there would be something ready on Thursday.
The window was left open all night, so that the whole apartment smelled like rain.
So that nobody would be left out, they made the party a potluck.
entries.русский: чтобы — основной союз цели; запятая перед ним меняет смысл на «так что» (результат)
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of purpose, or of result when preceded by a comma
entries.pattern: [main clause] so that [clause with modal]. — purpose · [main clause], so that [clause]. — result · So that [clause], [main clause]. — fronted, formal
entries.punctuation: The central rule of this category. ✗ No comma before so that = purpose: He spoke slowly so that everyone would understand (that was the goal). ✗ Comma before so that = result: He spoke slowly, so that everyone understood (that is what happened). A semicolon is always wrong here.
entries.variants: so (that-dropped, informal)
entries.see also: so, in order that, in order to, so as to, so ... that, lest

entries.meaning: Bare that as a purpose subordinator survives in scripture, hymns, oratory, poetry, and deliberate archaism: Come, that we may see. Only the purpose that pairs with may or might, which is the test for spotting it, because the same word does four commoner jobs: the complementizer that opens a noun clause (I know that he left), the relative pronoun (the book that I read), the demonstrative determiner and pronoun (that book, give me that), and the degree adverb of informal speech (It wasn't that cold).
examples: Speak plainly, that all may understand.
He gave up his seat that the older woman might sit down.
Come closer, that we may see your face.
They fought that their children might live free.
Write these things down, that the record be preserved.
She worked all her life that her name might outlast her.
entries.русский: дабы, чтобы — устар., книжн. союз цели, только в паре с may/might
entries.pattern: [main clause] that [subject] may/might [verb]. · [imperative], that [subject] may/might [verb]. · [main clause] that [subject] [bare subjunctive verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma is required, and none appears when the purpose clause is the point of the sentence (He gave up his seat that she might sit down). A comma is usual after an imperative or a short main clause, where the purpose clause reads as an added statement of aim (Speak plainly, that all may understand). Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate. Modern edited prose simply rewrites the whole thing as so that.
entries.variants: so that and in order that are the modern equivalents
entries.see also: so that, in order that, to the end that, lest

entries.ipa: /tə ði ˈɛnd ðæt/, reduced /tə ði ˈɛnd ðət/
entries.meaning: A ceremonial in order that, at home in statutes, contracts, charters, and older sermons and nowhere else. End here means "purpose, goal," not "finish," which is what makes the phrase opaque to learners. In any ordinary sentence, write so that.
examples: The board publishes its minutes, to the end that the public may follow its work.
Records shall be retained for seven years to the end that an audit may be conducted.
The treaty was drafted to the end that neither party could later claim surprise.
He endowed the chair to the end that the subject might never be dropped from the curriculum.
All parties shall cooperate, to the end that the transfer may close on schedule.
The rules are circulated in advance to the end that no member is taken unawares.
To the end that the fund may continue in perpetuity, the trustees shall reinvest all income.
entries.русский: с тем чтобы, дабы — юр., книжн.; end здесь «цель», а не «конец»
entries.pattern: [main clause] to the end that [clause with modal]. · [main clause], to the end that [clause with modal]. · To the end that [clause with modal], [main clause]. — rare
entries.punctuation: A comma before it is common in legal drafting, where the clause states an added aim; leave the comma out when the purpose clause is essential to the sentence. Comma after the clause in the rare fronted order. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate.
entries.variants: to the intent that (legal, rarer)
entries.see also: in order that, to the intent that, so that, that, to which end, whereby

entries.ipa: /tə ði ɪnˈtɛnt ðæt/, reduced /tə ði ɪnˈtɛnt ðət/
entries.meaning: An American meets this one in old deeds, wills, and trust instruments, in English conveyancing precedents, and in nineteenth-century statutes and charters — never in modern American drafting, which writes with the intent that or plain so that. It differs from its twin to the end that only in what the noun names: end names the goal aimed at, while intent names what was in the drafter's mind, which is why this version outlived the other in instruments where somebody's intention is itself the operative fact. The clause takes may, might, or shall, or occasionally the bare present subjunctive.
examples: The lands are conveyed to the trustees, to the intent that the same may be sold and the proceeds divided among my children.
This release is given to the intent that no further claim shall be made upon the estate.
I give my library to the parish, to the intent that it may be kept together and lent to any inhabitant.
The Act was passed to the intent that the ancient rights of common might be preserved to the freeholders.
The shares were transferred into her name alone, to the intent that she should take the whole beneficially.
Notice shall be published for three weeks, to the intent that no creditor may afterwards plead ignorance of the proceeding.
The parties have set their hands hereunto, to the intent and purpose that the covenants herein may bind their heirs and assigns.
entries.русский: с тем намерением, чтобы — устар. юр., язык старых завещаний и актов
entries.register: archaic legal — conveyancing and drafting boilerplate
entries.pattern: [main clause], to the intent that [clause with may/might/shall]. · [main clause] to the intent that [clause with may/might/shall]. · [main clause] to the intent and purpose that [clause]. — the doubled drafting formula · To the intent that [clause], [main clause]. — rare
entries.punctuation: A comma before it is the drafting norm, because the purpose clause is hung on a provision that is already complete; leave the comma out when the purpose restricts the main clause rather than commenting on it. Comma after the clause in the rare fronted order. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate, not independent.
entries.variants: to the intent and purpose that, to the end that (the commoner twin), with the intent that (the modern American drafting equivalent)
entries.see also: to the end that, with the intent that, in order that, so that, to which end

entries.meaning: The relative twin of to that end: it reaches back, treats the whole preceding clause as the goal, and then names the step taken to reach it. End here means "purpose," exactly as in to the end that, and not "finish." It belongs to charters, trusts, and contracts; in ordinary prose start a new sentence with to that end.
examples: The trust must be preserved in perpetuity, to which end the trustees shall reinvest all income.
The parties wish to close by March 1, to which end each shall deliver its schedules within ten days.
The society was founded to keep the language alive, to which end it runs a summer school every July.
He meant the farm to pass to his grandchildren intact, to which end he broke none of it up in the will.
The council resolved to clear the backlog by fall, to which end two additional clerks were hired in April.
The charter directs the board to publish every vote, to which end the minutes go up within a week of each meeting.
entries.русский: с каковой целью, ради чего — книжн., юр.; отсылает к цели, названной в предыдущей части
entries.pattern: [independent clause], to which end [clause]. · [independent clause]. To which end, [clause]. · [independent clause], to which end [subject] shall/may [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma before it, never a semicolon and never nothing — it is a supplementary relative, so it takes the punctuation of which is why rather than the punctuation of therefore. A comma after it is optional and turns up mainly when the phrase opens a new sentence.
entries.variants: to that end, to this end (the demonstrative versions, which start a fresh sentence)
entries.see also: to the end that, in order that, whereby, which is why, to that end

entries.ipa: /wɪð ði ɪnˈtɛnt ðæt/, reduced /wɪð ði ɪnˈtɛnt ðət/
entries.meaning: States the actor's purpose as a matter of record, which is why it lives in statutes, wills, and pleadings: what is being asserted is what was in somebody's mind, not what actually came about. The clause takes a modal — would, should, might — or, in drafting, the present subjunctive: with the intent that the fund be divided equally. Its everyday relatives with the aim of and with the intention of take an -ing form and cannot govern a clause of their own.
examples: She signed the deed over in March with the intent that her sister would keep the house.
The clause was inserted with the intent that neither side could walk away without notice.
He transferred the shares with the intention that the dividends should fund the scholarship.
The photographs were released with the intent that they be read as evidence, not as art.
Congress wrote the exemption narrowly with the intent that only family farms would qualify.
He was charged with entering the building with intent to commit theft.
The memo went to every department with the intention that nobody could later plead ignorance.
entries.русский: с намерением, чтобы — юр.: фиксирует умысел действующего лица, а не итог
entries.pattern: [main clause] with the intent that [clause]. · [main clause] with the intention that [clause]. · [main clause] with intent to [base verb]. — the criminal-law formula · With the intent that [clause], [main clause]. — rare
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause, which is where it almost always sits. Comma after the clause in the rare fronted order. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate.
entries.variants: with the intention that, with intent to + base verb, with the object that (legalistic)
entries.see also: with the aim of, in order that, so that, to the end that, to the intent that, for the purpose of

entries.meaning: The purpose marker of statutes, contracts, and policy documents. It takes an -ing form and never an infinitive — for the purpose of collecting data, not for the purpose of to collect data. The for purposes of X variant does something slightly different: it limits a definition to one document or context.
examples: The data is retained for the purpose of verifying eligibility.
For the purpose of this agreement, "employee" includes independent contractors.
She entered the building for the purpose of serving the summons.
The fund was created for the purpose of rebuilding the pier.
Cameras were installed for the purpose of deterring theft, not monitoring staff.
For purposes of the tax code, the two entities are treated as one.
entries.русский: с целью, для — книжн., юр.; дальше только -ing или существительное, не инфинитив
entries.pattern: [main clause] for the purpose of [gerund phrase]. · For the purpose of [gerund phrase], [main clause]. · For purposes of [noun], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted.
entries.variants: for purposes of, for the purposes of
entries.see also: in order to, so as to, to, with a view to, with the aim of

entries.ipa: /fɚ ðə ˈseɪk əv/, reduced /fɚ ðə ˈseɪk ə/
entries.meaning: Purpose named through the person or thing that benefits — for the sake of the kids — or through the quality being served, as in for the sake of clarity. It takes a noun or an -ing form and never an infinitive. Two things sit next to it and are not it: the possessive shortcut for her own sake, which is the same construction turned inside out, and the exasperated interjection for heaven's sake, which names no goal at all.
examples: They stayed in the same city for the sake of the kids.
For the sake of clarity, the report uses the 2019 boundaries throughout.
She learned the software for the sake of keeping the job, not because she liked it.
Both sides agreed to a short recess for the sake of letting tempers cool.
Don't rewrite the whole chapter for the sake of one sentence.
For the sake of argument, suppose the early numbers are right.
He gave up the corner office for his partner's sake.
entries.русский: ради, для блага — цель через того или то, что от неё выигрывает
entries.type: quasi-subordinator (prepositional, takes a noun or a gerund)
entries.clause type: non-finite purpose adjunct (noun or gerund phrase)
entries.pattern: [main clause] for the sake of [noun/gerund]. · For the sake of [noun/gerund], [main clause]. · [main clause] for [possessive] sake. · For the sake of argument, [main clause]. — frozen hedge
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted, which is common. Never a semicolon — a phrase follows, not an independent clause.
entries.variants: for [possessive] sake (for the children's sake), for the sake of argument, for goodness' sake (interjection, not purpose)
entries.see also: in the interest of, for the purpose of, with the aim of, in order to, so that

entries.meaning: A doubled purpose marker — the preposition for stacked on the infinitive to — that was ordinary in Middle and Early Modern English and survives now only in ballads, the King James Bible, Appalachian and Southern regional speech, and Irish and Scots English. The trap is the standard pattern that looks like it: in He waited for the rain to stop a subject sits between the two words and the sentence is unremarkable, while He waited for to see her is dialect. In edited American prose, write plain to.
examples: We come for to sing you a song about the river.
He went down to the courthouse for to pay the fine himself.
A sower went out for to sow his seed.
She saved all winter for to buy the ticket home.
They gathered on the bank for to watch the boats come in.
I only stopped by for to say goodbye before the train.
The old ballad has him riding out for to seek his fortune.
entries.русский: чтобы — устар., диал.; язык баллад и южных говоров, в норме просто to
entries.pattern: [main clause] for to [base verb]. · [main clause] for to [base verb] [object]. · [verb of motion] for to [base verb]. — the commonest frame
entries.punctuation: No comma before it. It does not front, and it never takes a semicolon.
entries.variants: plain to and in order to are the standard equivalents; for [subject] to [verb] is a different and fully standard pattern
entries.see also: to, in order to, so as to, that, to the end that

entries.ipa: /ɪn ən ˈɛfɚt tu/, reduced /ɪn ən ˈɛfɚt tə/
entries.meaning: Purpose with a hedge built in. In order to and so as to simply name the aim; in an effort to reports that somebody was trying, and quietly declines to say it worked, which is why reporters reach for it when the outcome is still open or has already failed. Like every infinitival purpose marker it borrows the subject of the main clause, so the person making the effort has to be the person in the main clause. In a bid to is the compressed newspaper version and sounds odd outside a headline or a lede.
examples: The city cut fares in half in an effort to get riders back on the buses.
In an effort to clear the backlog, the clinic added Saturday hours.
Growers flooded the fields in an attempt to keep the frost off the buds.
He rewrote his resume three times in an effort to get past the screening software.
The league changed the overtime rule in an effort to cut down on head injuries.
In an attempt to settle before trial, both sides agreed to one more day of mediation.
entries.русский: пытаясь, в стремлении — газетный оборот: попытка, об успехе которой ничего не сказано
entries.register: neutral; the house style of American news writing
entries.pattern: [main clause] in an effort to [base verb]. · In an effort to [base verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] in an attempt to [base verb]. · [main clause] in a bid to [base verb]. — headline register
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted, which is common in reporting. Never a semicolon — an infinitive phrase follows, not an independent clause.
entries.variants: in an attempt to, in a bid to (headlinese), in hopes of + gerund
entries.see also: in order to, so as to, with the aim of, to, for the purpose of

entries.meaning: The explicit, slightly formal version of the plain purpose infinitive to. Its real value is disambiguation: He wrote to the senator is unclear, He wrote in order to reach the senator is not. The negative is in order not to — careful writing puts not before to, though in order to not is common in speech. Use in order for X to Y when the two clauses have different subjects.
examples: He took a second job in order to pay off the loan faster.
In order to qualify, applicants must have lived in the county for a year.
She left the office at four in order not to hit rush hour.
The store closed early in order for the staff to attend the funeral.
We rewrote the opening in order to make the point in the first paragraph.
In order to be safe, back up the drive before you run the update.
entries.русский: чтобы, для того чтобы — явный маркер цели перед инфинитивом
entries.pattern: [main clause] in order to [base verb]. · In order to [base verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] in order not to [base verb]. · [main clause] in order for [subject] to [base verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted in order to phrase. No comma when it follows the main clause.
entries.variants: in order not to, in order for ... to
entries.see also: to, so as to, in order that, so that, for the purpose of, in an effort to

entries.meaning: Names the value or the party a decision is meant to serve: in the interest of safety, in the interest of the shareholders. It takes a noun or an -ing form and never an infinitive. It also carries a faint note of justification, which is why it turns up in announcements, rulings, and apologies — places where somebody is explaining a decision that not everyone is going to like. The plural in the interests of is equally standard in American English.
examples: In the interest of time, we'll take two more questions and then break.
The hearing was closed in the interest of protecting the witnesses.
The airline canceled the flight in the interest of safety after the second warning light.
In the interests of full disclosure, I should say the author is a friend of mine.
The board sold the building in the interest of the membership, over the staff's objections.
He dropped the appeal in the interest of getting back to work.
entries.русский: в интересах, ради — называет ценность или сторону, которой служит решение
entries.type: quasi-subordinator (prepositional, takes a noun or a gerund)
entries.clause type: non-finite purpose adjunct (noun or gerund phrase)
entries.pattern: [main clause] in the interest of [noun/gerund]. · In the interest of [noun/gerund], [main clause]. · [main clause] in the interests of [noun]. · In the public interest, [main clause]. — fixed phrase
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted, which is the commoner order. Never a semicolon.
entries.variants: in the interests of, in the public interest, in the interest of [somebody's] safety/privacy/time
entries.see also: for the sake of, for the purpose of, with a view to, with the aim of, in an effort to

entries.meaning: A formal equivalent of in order to that is most alive in its negative, so as not to, which is the natural American way to say "in order to avoid." Like every infinitival purpose marker it shares the subject of the main clause; if the person acting and the person affected are different, you need so that.
examples: He rewrote the email so as to sound less annoyed.
She closed the door quietly so as not to wake the baby.
The trail loops north so as to avoid the private property.
Fold the paper in thirds so as to fit it in the envelope.
They scheduled the vote for Monday so as not to conflict with the holiday.
So as to keep the discussion short, the chair set a three-minute limit.
entries.русский: чтобы, так чтобы — книжн.; особенно частотна форма so as not to «чтобы не»
entries.register: neutral to formal — the negative so as not to is everyday American
entries.pattern: [main clause] so as to [base verb]. · [main clause] so as not to [base verb]. · So as to [base verb], [main clause]. — rare
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase in the rare fronted order.
entries.variants: so as not to
entries.see also: in order to, to, so that, so, in order that

entries.meaning: The plain to-infinitive is the ordinary, unmarked way to state purpose in American English — I came to help simply means "in order to help," and adding in order changes nothing but the formality. Switch to the longer forms only when the bare infinitive could be misread as a complement or a result, as in He stopped to talk (purpose) beside He stopped talking (aspect). Keep the infinitive marker apart from the preposition spelled the same way: in to the coast and listen to me, to takes a noun phrase and states direction or a target, while the purpose to takes a bare verb — which is why look forward to is followed by an -ing form (to leaving), a preposition and not this word at all.
examples: I stayed late to finish the quarterly report.
To get the discount, enter the code at checkout.
She called the vet to ask about the dosage.
We drove out to the coast to watch the meteor shower.
He raised his hand to get the waiter's attention.
They cut every other line item to keep the doors open.
I'm telling you this to explain what happened, not to excuse it.
entries.русский: чтобы — обычный инфинитив цели; не путать с предлогом to «к, в, на» перед существительным
entries.pattern: [main clause] to [base verb]. · To [base verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] to [base verb], not to [base verb]. — contrastive · [main clause] only to [base verb]. — unexpected result
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted purpose infinitive: To save time, we skipped lunch. No comma when it follows the main clause. A comma does appear before a contrastive second infinitive (to explain, not to excuse) and before only to.
entries.variants: in order to and so as to are the explicit forms
entries.see also: in order to, so as to, for the purpose of, so that, only to, too ... to

entries.ipa: /wɪð ə ˈvju tu/, reduced /wɪð ə ˈvju tə/, also /wɪθ/
entries.meaning: Business and diplomatic register, marking a longer-range aim than in order to. The to here is a preposition, so what follows has to be an -ing form — with a view to expanding, never with a view to expand. That is one of the most reliably repeated errors in formal English writing, and with an eye to behaves exactly the same way.
examples: The firm opened a Denver office with a view to expanding into the mountain states.
They restructured the debt with a view to refinancing it next spring.
She started taking night classes with an eye to changing careers.
The talks resumed with a view toward a cease-fire by June.
He saved every receipt with an eye to the audit he assumed was coming.
The land was purchased with a view to building a school on it.
With a view to cutting turnover, the hospital rewrote its whole scheduling policy.
entries.русский: с прицелом на, в расчёте на — офиц.; дальняя цель, дальше обязательно -ing
entries.pattern: [main clause] with a view to [gerund phrase]. · With a view to [gerund phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] with an eye to [gerund phrase or noun].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase in the less common fronted order, like any fronted adjunct. A comma in the normal order is acceptable only when the phrase is tacked on as an afterthought.
entries.variants: with a view toward, with an eye to, with an eye toward
entries.see also: with the aim of, for the purpose of, in order to, so as to

entries.meaning: States the actor's declared objective, and is the workhorse of journalism, grant writing, and reports. It takes an -ing form. Choose with the intention of when you want to stress what was in the actor's mind rather than what the action achieved — it is the version that survives a failed plan.
examples: The program was launched with the aim of cutting emergency-room visits.
With the goal of finishing by June, they brought on a second crew.
He moved to Austin with the intention of starting a business.
The amendment was written with the aim of closing exactly that loophole.
She entered the race with the goal of breaking three hours.
They bought the old bank with the intention of converting it into apartments.
entries.русский: с целью — называет заявленную цель действующего лица, дальше -ing
entries.pattern: [main clause] with the aim of [gerund phrase]. · With the aim of [gerund phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] with the intention of [gerund phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause. Comma after the phrase when it is fronted.
entries.variants: with the goal of, with the intention of, with the object of (legalistic)
entries.see also: with a view to, with the intent that, for the purpose of, in order to, in an effort to

entries.meaning: Points back at a goal, a fact, or a constraint just stated, and marks what follows as the step taken in view of it. It is the everyday version of to that end, and looser: to that end needs a goal in front of it, while with this in mind can point back at any consideration at all. It names no new purpose of its own, which is what separates it from every other phrase in this section.
examples: The grant runs out in June. With this in mind, the director has already started raising money for next year.
Most of our readers open the newsletter on a phone; with this in mind, we cut the images in half.
With that in mind, let's look at what happened in the second quarter.
The soil here drains fast. With this in mind, plant the lavender on the high side of the bed.
The committee wants a decision by Friday, and the agenda was written with that in mind.
Two of the panelists have never met the applicants. With this in mind, the chair asked for written summaries in advance.
entries.русский: с учётом этого, исходя из этого — отсылает к уже сказанному, новой цели не вводит
entries.type: linking adverbial (prepositional phrase functioning as a conjunctive adverb)
entries.clause type: independent clause (it does not subordinate anything)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]. With this in mind, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]; with this in mind, [independent clause]. · With that in mind, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb] ... with this in mind.
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it between two independent clauses, and a comma after it when it opens the clause. A comma alone in front of it is a comma splice. In the clause-final position — we wrote the policy with this in mind — it takes no punctuation at all.
entries.variants: with that in mind, bearing this in mind, keeping that in mind
entries.see also: with the aim of, in order to, accordingly, to that end, so that

entries.meaning: The positive counterpart of too ... to: the degree is sufficient, so the result does happen. The word-order rule is the trap, and it is absolute — enough follows an adjective or adverb (warm enough, clearly enough) but precedes a noun (enough chairs). Add for plus an object when the person doing the second verb is not the subject. The word floats across three classes, and the position tells you which one you have: adverb of degree after an adjective, determiner before a noun, and bare pronoun on its own (I've had enough).
examples: The water was warm enough to swim in by the second week of June.
He spoke loudly enough for the back row to hear every word.
We have enough chairs to seat forty people.
She was tired enough that she fell asleep in the car on the way home.
The ice looked thick enough to walk on, but nobody tried it.
He knows the city well enough to get around without a map.
It rained enough that the field behind the school flooded again.
entries.русский: достаточно ..., чтобы — степени хватает, и результат наступает
entries.clause type: non-finite result clause (to-infinitive); finite with that
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] [adjective/adverb] enough to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] enough [noun] to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] [adjective] enough for [object] to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] [adjective] enough that [clause]. · [subject] [verb] enough that [clause]. — bare adverb, no adjective in front of it
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere inside the construction, in any of its versions.
entries.variants: enough ... that, enough that (bare adverb after the verb), enough ... for ... to
entries.see also: too ... to, so ... as to, so ... that, such ... that, to such an extent that

entries.meaning: The infinitival twin of so ... that: the degree named in the first half is high enough to produce the result named in the second, but the result arrives as an infinitive instead of a finite clause. It is a step more formal than so ... that and lives in three places — technical description (so arranged as to prevent backflow), understatement with not (not so foolish as to sign it), and the frozen courtesy would you be so kind as to. Do not confuse it with the purpose marker so as to, which has no degree word standing in front of it: He moved the ladder so as to reach the gutter states an aim, while The gutter was so high as to be unreachable states a degree and its consequence.
examples: The vents sit so high as to be useless in a room this size.
He was not so careless as to leave the keys in the ignition.
The panels are fitted so tightly as to leave no gap for water.
Would you be so kind as to hold the door for a second?
Her answer was so vague as to tell us nothing at all.
The margin was so small as to fall inside the polling error.
The two accounts differ so sharply as to raise a question about the source.
entries.русский: настолько ..., что — книжн. вариант so ... that; be so kind as to «будьте добры»
entries.pattern: [subject] [be] so [adjective] as to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] so [adverb] as to [base verb]. · [subject] [be] not so [adjective] as to [base verb]. — understatement · Be so kind/good as to [base verb]. — frozen request formula
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere inside the construction, in any of its versions.
entries.variants: such ... as to, not so ... as to
entries.see also: so ... that, so as to, such ... that, too ... to, enough ... to

entries.meaning: Marks a degree high enough to produce a result. So attaches to an adjective or an adverb; the same job for a whole noun phrase belongs to such — so cold that beside such a cold night that. With a noun you have to insert a quantity word: so many applicants, not so applicants.
examples: The line was so long that we gave up and ate at home.
She talks so fast that I miss about half of it.
There were so many applicants that the website crashed twice.
He was so tired he fell asleep with his shoes on.
The room got so quiet that you could hear the clock in the hall.
So thick was the fog that the ferries stopped running altogether.
entries.русский: так, настолько ..., что — степень и её следствие; so при прилагательном или наречии
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] so [adjective/adverb] that [result clause]. · [subject] [verb] so much/many/little/few [noun] that [result clause]. · So [adjective] [be] [subject] that [result clause]. — literary inversion
entries.punctuation: No comma before that. When that is dropped in speech and informal writing, a comma often takes its place: It was so loud, I left.
entries.variants: so ... (that) with that dropped, so much ... that, so many ... that, so little ... that, so few ... that
entries.see also: such ... that, such that, so much so that, so ... as to, so that, so, too ... to, enough ... to

entries.meaning: The noun-phrase counterpart of so ... that: use it when the degree word has to attach to a noun rather than to a bare adjective. Article order is where learners slip — such a good movie, never a such good movie — and note that the so version flips the article to the other side: so good a movie, which is formal but correct.
examples: It was such a good movie that we watched it again the next night.
They serve such enormous portions that nobody ever orders dessert.
He spoke with such confidence that no one questioned the numbers.
The storm did such damage that the school stayed closed for a week.
Such was the noise from the street that we moved the table to the back patio.
She had such a headache that she left work before noon.
entries.русский: такой ..., что — то же, что so ... that, но при существительном
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] such a/an [adjective] [singular noun] that [result clause]. · [subject] [verb] such [plural or mass noun] that [result clause]. · Such [be] [noun] that [result clause]. — formal inversion
entries.punctuation: No comma before that.
entries.variants: such a ... that with singular count nouns
entries.see also: so ... that, such that, so that

entries.meaning: Excess that blocks a result: too tired to think means "so tired that I can't think." Two things follow from the negation being locked inside too. The infinitive stays positive — too heavy to lift, never too heavy not to lift — and the object slot at the end stays empty: The soup is too hot to drink, with no it after drink. With a singular count noun the article moves in behind the adjective, exactly as it does after so: too big a risk to take. Keep the degree word apart from the other too, the sentence adverb meaning "also" (I'm coming too), which never sets up a following infinitive.
examples: I'm too tired to argue about this tonight.
The box was too heavy for one person to carry up the stairs.
It's too early to tell whether the treatment is working.
He was driving too fast to stop at the light.
There were too many variables to draw any conclusion.
The coffee is still too hot to drink.
Buying at that price was too big a risk to take on one appraisal.
entries.русский: слишком ..., чтобы — избыток, из-за которого действие не выходит; отрицание уже в too
entries.clause type: non-finite result clause (to-infinitive), negative in force
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] too [adjective/adverb] to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] too [adjective] for [object] to [base verb]. · [subject] [verb] too much/many [noun] to [base verb]. · [subject] [be] too [adjective] a [singular noun] to [base verb]. — article inversion
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere inside the construction.
entries.variants: too ... for ... to, too ... a ... to
entries.see also: enough ... to, so ... as to, so ... that, such ... that, to

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈsʌtʃ ə ˈweɪ ðæt/, reduced /ɪn ˈsʌtʃ ə ˈweɪ ðət/
entries.meaning: Manner and result folded into one phrase: it says how something was done and, in the same breath, what that manner brought about. It is the long form of such that, and the choice between them is register — Arrange the panels such that no two identical colors touch is technical, and in such a way that is the version that reads naturally in ordinary prose. In such a manner that is the drafting variant and belongs to specifications, codes, and contracts.
examples: Stack the boxes in such a way that the labels all face the aisle.
The question was worded in such a way that a yes could later be read as a no.
He resigned in such a way that nobody could accuse him of walking out on the project.
The rear seats fold in such a way as to leave the floor completely flat.
Fixtures shall be mounted in such a manner that they can be serviced without removing the ceiling.
She told the story in a way that made everyone at the table the hero of one line.
The bylaws were rewritten in such a way that no single member can block a vote.
entries.русский: таким образом, что; так, чтобы — способ действия и его результат в одном обороте
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of manner and result
entries.pattern: [main clause] in such a way that [clause]. · [main clause] in such a way as to [base verb]. · [main clause] in such a manner that [clause]. — formal · [main clause] in a way that [clause]. — plainer
entries.punctuation: No comma before it. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate, not independent.
entries.variants: in such a manner that (formal, legal), in such a way as to + base verb, in a way that (plainer)
entries.see also: such that, so that, so ... as to, to such an extent that, whereby

entries.meaning: Marks what comes next as a conclusion forced by what came before. Grammatically it is not a conjunction at all — it is a dummy subject, follows is the verb, and the that-clause is that verb's complement — but it does a conjunction's work in argument, standing where therefore would stand and carrying more logical weight. Its most useful shape is the negative: it does not follow that is the standard way to reject an inference without disputing the premise it was drawn from.
examples: Every witness was inside the building at nine. It follows that none of them saw the car leave.
The two sets have the same number of elements; it follows that a one-to-one pairing exists.
The contract was never signed, and it follows that neither party is bound by it.
She was on a plane all afternoon. It follows that she could not have sent the message at four.
The sample came from a single county, so it does not follow that the result holds statewide.
If the earlier reading is correct, it would follow that the manuscript predates the fire.
From this it follows that the second experiment was measuring something else entirely.
entries.русский: отсюда следует, что — вывод, вынуждаемый сказанным; отриц. «отсюда не следует, что»
entries.clause type: independent clause with a that-clause complement
entries.pattern: [independent clause]. It follows that [clause]. · [independent clause]; it follows that [clause]. · [independent clause], and it follows that [clause]. · From this it follows that [clause]. · It does not follow that [clause]. — the negative, which does most of the work
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it, because it opens a full independent clause of its own — or a coordinating conjunction plus a comma, which is the ordinary way to join two independent clauses. A comma by itself is a comma splice. No comma after that, and none before it.
entries.variants: from this it follows that, it would follow that (hedged), it does not follow that (negative)
entries.see also: therefore, thus, which means, consequently, as a corollary

entries.meaning: Spells out the consequence, or the plain-English translation, of what was just said. It is the participial cousin of which means, and the two are close to interchangeable, with one difference of feel: which means draws a conclusion, while meaning more often restates the point in words the reader can act on. Keep the connector apart from the ordinary participle after a noun — a sign meaning "no entry" — which glosses a single word instead of the whole clause.
examples: The office closes at four on Fridays, meaning you'll have to file the form on Monday.
The tunnel is down to one lane, meaning that the detour adds twenty minutes each way.
She's the only signer on the account — meaning nothing moves without her.
The rate is fixed for five years, meaning that the payment will not change until 2031.
Two of the three servers sit in the same building, meaning one outage takes both of them down.
The deposit is nonrefundable, meaning you lose it if you cancel for any reason at all.
He came in second by a tenth of a second, meaning he missed the final by one place.
entries.русский: то есть, а значит — поясняет следствие сказанного простыми словами
entries.clause type: supplementary participial clause of result or restatement
entries.pattern: [independent clause], meaning [clause]. · [independent clause], meaning that [clause]. · [independent clause] — meaning [noun phrase]. · [noun phrase], meaning [noun phrase]. — gloss
entries.punctuation: A comma or a dash before it, always; never a semicolon, because what follows is a participial phrase rather than an independent clause. No comma after meaning. The that is optional and is normally dropped in speech.
entries.variants: which means, meaning + noun phrase (gloss), which is to say (formal)
entries.see also: which means, which is why, thereby, with the result that, so

entries.meaning: The disappointment infinitive. It has the shape of a purpose infinitive but reports the opposite: not what the subject was aiming at, but what actually happened, and what happened defeated the effort just described. He drove four hours to see the exhibit is purpose; He drove four hours, only to find it closed is result, and an unwelcome one. Switch to only for X to Y when the person let down is not the one who acted. Keep this only apart from the far commoner focusing adverb (only on Tuesdays, I only asked), which never sets up an infinitive.
examples: She sprinted the length of the terminal, only to watch the plane push back from the gate.
We repainted the whole kitchen, only to decide a month later that we hated the color.
He saved for two years, only to have the tuition raised again in April.
The crew rebuilt the deck in October, only for a storm to take it out in January.
I called the office three times, only to get the same recording.
The council passed the ordinance in June, only to repeal it before it ever took effect.
We drove all the way out to the orchard, only to find that it had closed for the season.
entries.русский: и в итоге лишь..., только чтобы (обнаружить) — неожиданный и обидный исход вместо цели
entries.pattern: [independent clause], only to [base verb]. · [independent clause], only to find/discover/learn [that-clause]. · [independent clause], only to have [object] [past participle]. · [independent clause], only for [subject] to [base verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma before only to, and here the comma is required rather than optional, because the phrase comments on the whole clause instead of naming the aim of the verb. Never a semicolon: what follows is an infinitive phrase, not an independent clause.
entries.variants: only for ... to (when the subjects differ), only to have + object
entries.see also: to, in order to, with the result that, which is why

entries.ipa: /ˌsoʊ ˈmʌtʃ soʊ ðæt/, reduced /ˌsoʊ ˈmʌtʃ soʊ ðət/
entries.meaning: The pro-form of so ... that. Split so ... that wraps around the degree word (so spicy that I couldn't finish it); so much so that leaves the degree word where it stands in the first clause and then points back at it (It was spicy, so much so that I couldn't finish it). The middle so is doing pro-form duty — it stands in for whatever adjective just appeared — which is why the phrase looks like a stutter and is not one. Reach for it when the adjective sits too far back for the split construction to reach, or when the result deserves its own beat.
examples: The room was cold, so much so that we could see our breath.
Turnout was down, so much so that two precincts closed an hour early.
She has reread the book maybe thirty times — so much so that she quotes it in ordinary conversation.
Rents climbed all spring, so much so that the council called an emergency session.
He was convincing, so much so that nobody thought to check the dates.
The trail is popular now, so much so that the lot fills by seven on Saturdays.
"Is the neighborhood really that expensive?" "So much so."
entries.русский: настолько, что — отсылает назад к степени, названной в предыдущей части фразы
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of result, hanging on a degree already stated
entries.pattern: [clause containing an adjective or adverb], so much so that [result clause]. · [clause] — so much so that [result clause]. · [clause], so much so. — result left implied
entries.punctuation: A comma or a dash before it, always. Unlike split so ... that, it cannot sit tight against the word it measures, because it is reaching back to a degree stated in the previous clause. Never a semicolon — the clause it introduces is subordinate. No comma after it.
entries.variants: so much so used alone
entries.see also: so ... that, such ... that, to the point that, such that, with the result that

entries.meaning: Two jobs in one phrase. In ordinary prose it reports result: the state of affairs was of a kind that produced what follows. In mathematics, logic, and technical writing it states the condition an object has to satisfy — a number x such that x squared is four. Keep it distinct from split such ... that, where such modifies a noun earlier in the sentence and that comes later.
examples: Arrange the panels such that no two identical colors touch.
The lighting in the room was such that every photo came out orange.
Choose a value of n such that the sum is divisible by three.
His schedule is such that we only overlap on Thursday mornings.
The wording was changed such that both readings are now defensible.
Set the timer such that the pump runs an hour before sunrise.
entries.русский: такой, что; так, чтобы — книжн., тех.; в математике «такой, что» при задании условия
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of result, or a specification clause after a noun
entries.pattern: [main clause] such that [clause]. · [noun phrase] such that [clause]. — mathematical specification
entries.punctuation: No comma before such that in either use.
entries.see also: such ... that, so that, in such a way that, with the result that, whereby

entries.ipa: /tə ˈsʌtʃ ən ɪkˈstɛnt ðæt/, reduced /tə ˈsʌtʃ ən ɪkˈstɛnt ðət/
entries.meaning: The formal member of the so ... that family. Where so ... that wraps around a single adjective and to the point that names a threshold that was crossed, to such an extent that measures the whole action, which is why it belongs to reports and academic prose. Do not swap in to the extent that: dropping such changes the meaning completely, because that phrase means "insofar as" and states a condition rather than an outcome.
examples: The river silted up to such an extent that barges could no longer reach the mill.
Costs rose to such an extent that the second phase was abandoned before it broke ground.
He has revised the opening to such a degree that almost nothing of the first draft is left in it.
The building had settled to such an extent that none of the doors closed properly.
Attendance fell to such a degree that the festival was called off after twenty-one years.
The species has recovered to such an extent that it came off the protected list last spring.
The two dialects have diverged to such an extent that speakers now watch each other's films with subtitles.
entries.русский: до такой степени, что — книжн.; не путать с to the extent that «постольку, поскольку»
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of result at a degree
entries.pattern: [main clause] to such an extent that [clause]. · [main clause] to such a degree that [clause]. · [main clause], to such an extent that [clause]. · To such an extent [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] that [clause]. — literary inversion
entries.punctuation: Usually no comma. Writers add one when the result reads as a separate escalation rather than as part of the same measurement, exactly as with to the point that. Never a semicolon — the clause is subordinate.
entries.variants: to such a degree that, to such a point that, to the extent that (which states a condition, not a result)
entries.see also: to the point that, so ... that, so much so that, such that, in such a way that

entries.ipa: /tə ðə ˈpɔɪnt ðæt/, reduced /tə ðə ˈpɔɪnt ðət/
entries.meaning: Names a threshold the situation crossed, so the result comes across as an extreme rather than a simple consequence. It overlaps with so ... that but attaches to the whole clause instead of to a single adjective, which makes it the natural choice when the escalation is gradual. To the point where is the more conversational of the two.
examples: The noise went on to the point that neighbors started calling the police.
She reworked the essay to the point where it no longer sounded like her.
Prices rose to the point that people simply stopped eating out.
He apologized to the point of embarrassment.
The software slowed down to the point where it was faster to do it by hand.
They rehearsed to the point that nobody needed a script.
entries.русский: до того, что; до такой степени, что — порог, который ситуация перешла
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of result at a threshold
entries.pattern: [main clause] to the point that [clause]. · [main clause] to the point where [clause]. · [main clause] to the point of [gerund/noun].
entries.punctuation: Usually no comma. Writers add one when the clause reads as a separate escalation: It rained all week, to the point that the field flooded.
entries.variants: to the point where, to the point of + gerund or noun
entries.see also: so ... that, such that, so much so that, to such an extent that, with the result that

entries.meaning: Means "by means of which" or "as a result of which," and it always hangs on a preceding noun that names a mechanism — a deal, a policy, a scheme, a process. It cannot modify a whole clause and it cannot open a sentence, which is what separates it from a general result connector. If you cannot name the mechanism noun, write by which or recast the sentence.
examples: They reached an agreement whereby the city would maintain the trail.
The company has a policy whereby unused vacation days roll over one year.
Congress created a program whereby borrowers could refinance at a fixed rate.
There is an unwritten rule whereby the last person out locks up.
The settlement set up a process whereby claims are reviewed by an outside panel.
He described a scheme whereby the same votes would be counted twice.
The 1997 consent decree, whereby the state took over the fund, expires next year.
entries.русский: посредством чего, согласно которому — книжн., юр.; всегда при существительном-механизме
entries.clause type: relative clause of means or result
entries.pattern: [noun naming a mechanism: agreement, rule, system, process, plan] whereby [clause]. — defining, no comma · [fully identified noun], whereby [clause]. — supplementary, comma · [main clause] under/by [determiner] [noun naming a mechanism] whereby [clause]. — the prepositional frame it most often sits in
entries.punctuation: No comma before whereby when the clause defines the noun, which is the normal case. Use a comma only when the clause is a supplementary aside about a noun already fully identified: the 1997 settlement, whereby the state took over the fund. Never a semicolon, and it can never open a sentence.
entries.variants: by which is the plainer equivalent; by means of which is the full form the word compresses; by means of + noun is the bare preposition behind both and joins no clauses at all
entries.see also: such that, thereby, with the result that, to the end that

entries.meaning: Reaches back and treats the entire preceding clause as the reason for what comes next. In meaning it works like therefore; in grammar it is a relative clause, which is why it is punctuated with a comma rather than the semicolon a conjunctive adverb would demand. It is also the most conversational result connector in this file.
examples: The bridge was closed all morning, which is why everybody showed up late.
She grew up bilingual, which is why the accent fooled me.
Our server sits in Oregon, which is why the timestamps look three hours off.
He never reads the group chat, which is why he came on the wrong day.
The recipe has no eggs in it, which is how it stays vegan.
They cut the budget back in March, which is why there is no summer program.
Nobody signed off on the change, which is the reason it never made it into the release notes.
entries.русский: поэтому, вот почему — относит. оборот: всё сказанное перед ним — причина
entries.type: relative (sentential), used as a result connector
entries.pattern: [independent clause], which is why [clause]. · [independent clause], which is how [clause]. · [independent clause], which is the reason [clause]. · [independent clause] — which is why [clause].
entries.punctuation: Always a comma before it, never a semicolon and never nothing. It is a supplementary relative clause, so the comma is both required and sufficient — the opposite of the rule for therefore.
entries.variants: which is how, which is the reason
entries.see also: which means, therefore, consequently, as a result, only to, so

entries.meaning: Reaches back, treats the whole preceding clause as a premise, and states what follows from it. It is the conversational therefore. Its neighbor which is why looks almost identical and runs the other direction: which is why says the first clause caused the second, while which means says the first clause proves the second.
examples: The last bus leaves at ten, which means we should order now.
Both accounts show the same login, which means one of them is not hers.
The deposit cleared this morning, which means that the funds are available today.
He's third on the list and the two people ahead of him withdrew, which means he's in.
The lease renews automatically in August, which would mean another year at this rent.
The battery is original, which means it holds about half the charge it used to.
Two inspectors are out sick — which means nothing ships before Thursday.
entries.русский: а значит, из чего следует — разговорный аналог therefore: вывод, а не причина
entries.type: relative (sentential), used as a result connector
entries.clause type: sentential relative clause of inference or consequence
entries.pattern: [independent clause], which means [clause]. · [independent clause], which means that [clause]. · [independent clause] — which means [noun phrase]. · [independent clause], which would mean [clause]. — hypothetical
entries.punctuation: Always a comma or a dash before it, never a semicolon and never nothing. It is a supplementary relative clause, so the comma is both required and sufficient. The that after it is optional and is usually dropped in speech.
entries.variants: which means that, which would mean, meaning (that)
entries.see also: which is why, meaning (that), it follows that, therefore, so

entries.ipa: /wɪð ðə rɪˈzʌlt ðæt/, reduced /wɪð ðə rɪˈzʌlt ðət/
entries.meaning: Labels what followed, in so many words. It belongs to reports, academic writing, and legal prose; in speech Americans say so. Unlike so that, it can never be read as purpose — it states an outcome and nothing else, which makes it useful precisely where so that would be ambiguous.
examples: The vendor missed two deadlines, with the result that the launch slipped to fall.
Rainfall was half the average, with the result that the reservoirs never refilled.
The form was redesigned last year, with the result that error rates fell by a third.
Two inspectors retired the same month, with the result that the backlog doubled.
Interest rates rose sharply, with the effect that refinancing dried up overnight.
The rule was never enforced, with the consequence that everyone ignored it.
entries.русский: в результате чего, так что — книжн.: называет только исход, целью прочитан быть не может
entries.pattern: [independent clause], with the result that [clause]. · [independent clause], with the effect that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before it. Never a semicolon: the clause is subordinate, so it cannot take the punctuation that therefore and consequently require.
entries.variants: with the consequence that, with the effect that
entries.see also: so that, such that, therefore, consequently, as a result

entries.meaning: "And so, in keeping with that." It is the most agentive of the result adverbs: therefore draws a conclusion, while accordingly says somebody took action in response. It also keeps a plain manner sense at the end of a clause, where it simply means "in the way just described."
examples: The forecast called for freezing rain; accordingly, the district canceled classes.
Sales fell for three straight quarters. Accordingly, the board froze hiring.
The statute is ambiguous; accordingly, the court turned to the legislative history.
We were told to expect a smaller crowd, and we planned accordingly.
The deadline moved up two weeks; the team, accordingly, dropped two features.
Accordingly, the motion is denied.
entries.русский: соответственно, и поэтому — книжн.: в ответ на сказанное были приняты меры
entries.clause type: independent clause (it does not subordinate anything)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; accordingly, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Accordingly, [independent clause]. · [subject], accordingly, [verb] ... · [subject] [verb] accordingly. — manner sense
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it joins two independent clauses, and a comma after it. A comma alone in front of it is a comma splice. In the clause-final manner use (planned accordingly) it takes no punctuation at all.
entries.see also: therefore, consequently, thus, hence, as a result

entries.meaning: Marks the next statement as a secondary consequence — something that falls out of the first result rather than being the point of it. That makes it narrower than consequently: a corollary is an extra that comes with a proof or a policy whether anyone wanted it or not, which is why the phrase is at home in mathematics, philosophy, and analytical writing and sounds stiff anywhere else.
examples: The theorem fixes the maximum at four; as a corollary, no five-color map can be minimal.
Remote work cut the commute. As a corollary, downtown lunch counters lost half their traffic.
The statute bars the agency from setting prices; as a corollary, it cannot set them indirectly through fees.
As a corollary of the merger, three regional offices will close in the spring.
The team drafted for defense and, as a corollary, scored fewer points for two straight seasons.
Every share is now held electronically; as a corollary, the transfer agent's paper vault stands empty.
entries.русский: как следствие, в качестве побочного вывода — книжн., науч.: попутное, не главное следствие
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (prepositional phrase functioning as one)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; as a corollary, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. As a corollary, [independent clause]. · As a corollary of [noun], [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb], as a corollary, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses, and a comma after it when it opens the clause. A comma alone in front of it is a comma splice. As a corollary of plus a noun is an ordinary prepositional phrase and follows the ordinary comma rules for one.
entries.variants: as a corollary of/to + noun, a corollary of that is, correspondingly (looser)
entries.see also: consequently, therefore, thus, accordingly, it follows that

entries.meaning: The plainest of the result connectives and the only one that sounds natural in email and speech, where thus and hence would sound stiff. Watch the two shapes: as a result connects clauses, while as a result of takes a noun phrase and cannot introduce a clause.
examples: The supplier raised prices twice; as a result, we changed vendors.
Two lanes were closed for repaving. As a result, the commute doubled.
She missed the filing deadline and lost the appeal as a result.
Attendance dropped sharply as a result of the schedule change.
The bridge reopened early; as a consequence, downtown traffic eased by Friday.
As a result, nobody trusted the numbers in the second report.
entries.русский: в результате, поэтому — самый нейтральный из результативных оборотов, годится и в речи
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (prepositional phrase functioning as one)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; as a result, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. As a result, [independent clause]. · [subject] [verb] ... as a result. · As a result of [noun], [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses, and a comma after it when it opens a clause. A comma alone before it is a comma splice. Clause-final as a result usually takes no comma, and as a result of plus a noun is a preposition that follows the ordinary comma rules for a phrase.
entries.variants: as a consequence, as a result of + noun (prepositional)
entries.see also: consequently, therefore, thus, accordingly, with the result that

entries.meaning: Marks the second clause as the effect of the first. It is interchangeable with therefore in most sentences, with a slight difference of flavor: therefore leans logical, drawing a conclusion, while consequently leans causal, reporting a real-world effect.
examples: The samples were contaminated; consequently, the study was withdrawn.
He never filed the paperwork. Consequently, the permit expired in April.
Snow closed the pass for two days; consequently, deliveries ran a week late.
The departments use different systems and, consequently, duplicate half their work.
Consequently, the committee recommends no change to the policy.
Funding was cut in March; consequently, the clinic reduced its hours.
entries.русский: следовательно, вследствие этого — книжн.: реальное последствие, а не логический вывод
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; consequently, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Consequently, [independent clause]. · [subject] and, consequently, [verb] ... · [subject] [auxiliary] consequently [verb] ...
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses, and a comma after it when it opens the clause. Joining two independent clauses with a comma plus consequently is a comma splice.
entries.variants: in consequence (formal, dated)
entries.see also: therefore, thus, hence, accordingly, as a result

entries.meaning: "For that reason, from this." Drier and more compressed than therefore, and its signature move is the verbless tag: The printer jammed twice, hence the delay. Do not confuse the result adverb with the time adverb spelled the same way, as in two weeks hence, which means "from now." From hence is redundant in both senses.
examples: The data was collected by volunteers; hence, some inconsistency is expected.
Both trains were canceled — hence the crowd on the platform.
The lease ends in June, hence the rush to find a subletter.
He grew up on the Chesapeake, hence the accent.
The bridge is one lane in each direction; hence, backups are routine.
Sample sizes were small, hence the wide confidence intervals.
The original files were lost in the move. Hence, the timeline had to be rebuilt from old emails.
entries.русский: отсюда, потому и — книжн.; часто без глагола: hence the delay «отсюда и задержка»
entries.clause type: independent clause; also used with no verb before a noun phrase
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; hence, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Hence, [independent clause]. · [independent clause], hence [noun phrase]. — verbless · [independent clause] — hence [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when a full clause follows, and the comma after it is optional. In the verbless pattern (hence the delay) a comma or a dash is enough, because what follows is not an independent clause and so needs no semicolon.
entries.see also: thus, thereby, therefore, consequently, accordingly

entries.meaning: Two jobs, told apart by intonation. In narrative it simply moves the story forward — So then she gets up and walks out — where it is barely more than a sequencing filler. In argument it draws an inference out of what the other person just said, very often as a question: So then you're saying it was my fault? Writers who want the inferential reading on the page often put a comma inside the phrase and print it so, then. Both uses belong to speech; in edited prose, use therefore, so, or next.
examples: The car wouldn't start. So then we called a cab and missed the first act anyway.
So then, you're telling me the invoice was never sent?
He said the office was closed. So then why is the light on?
She finished the coursework in June; so then the only thing left was the thesis.
So then the whole row of us had to stand up so she could get past.
So then, where does that leave the Friday deadline?
entries.русский: и вот тогда; так что же — разг.: в рассказе последовательность, в споре вывод-вопрос
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (discourse marker of inference and sequence)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]. So then, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. So then [independent clause]. — narrative, no comma · So then, [question]? — checking an inference · [independent clause]; so then [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it when it opens a new sentence. A comma in front of it is defensible only because the so inside it can serve as a coordinating conjunction; with the inferential reading, treat it like therefore and use the stronger stop. The comma after it is optional and is usually dropped in narrative.
entries.variants: and then (pure sequence), so anyway (resuming a story), bare so (the plain result conjunction)
entries.see also: so, therefore, accordingly, that way / this way, thus

entries.meaning: The spoken American answer to so that. It points back at the action just proposed and names the benefit that action buys: Write it on the calendar. That way you won't forget is Write it on the calendar so that you won't forget, split across two sentences. That way points at something already said, while this way points at what the speaker is proposing at that moment. Two lookalikes are not connectives at all — the manner phrase (hold the bracket that way) and the direction adverb (the restrooms are that way) — and neither one links a pair of clauses.
examples: Park behind the building. That way you won't have to feed the meter.
Send the draft tonight; that way, she can read it on the plane.
Let's split the list in half. This way, we're both done by five.
Freeze half the dough. That way there's a pizza ready on a Wednesday.
I put her number in my phone. That way, I don't have to dig out the card every time.
We could meet at the bakery instead — this way nobody has to drive downtown.
Label the cables before you unplug anything. That way you'll know what goes back where.
entries.русский: тогда, так — разг.: «сделай так — тогда не забудешь»; устная замена so that
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (noun phrase functioning as one)
entries.pattern: [independent clause]. That way, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]; that way, [independent clause]. · [imperative]. That way [independent clause]. · This way, [independent clause]. — pointing at a plan being proposed now
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it between two independent clauses, and a comma after it in careful writing, though speech and casual prose drop that comma routinely. A comma alone in front of it is a comma splice, the same error as with therefore.
entries.variants: this way, that way you (fixed conversational opener)
entries.see also: so that, so, so then, accordingly, to that end

entries.meaning: "By that means, and as a result of it." It is the adverb to whereby's relative: whereby has to hang on a noun that names a mechanism, while thereby points back at the whole preceding clause. Nearly all its modern life is spent in front of an -ing form, which is why the comma, not the semicolon, is its normal punctuation — writers who reach for it after a semicolon usually want thus or therefore instead. It also survives in the frozen idiom thereby hangs a tale, where it means "in connection with that."
examples: The company retired its two oldest plants, thereby cutting emissions by nearly a fifth.
The renewal clause was struck before signing, thereby leaving the contract silent on what happens in year four.
Each district drew its own map and thereby protected its own incumbents.
She paid the filing fee out of pocket, thereby keeping the appeal alive.
Blanch the greens first, thereby holding the color through a long braise.
The update caches the font locally and thereby removes one round trip from every page load.
entries.русский: тем самым — книжн., обычно перед оборотом с -ing, а не перед целым предложением
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (result by means of what was just said)
entries.clause type: heads an -ing participial phrase; rarely a full independent clause
entries.pattern: [independent clause], thereby [-ing participle phrase]. · [subject] [verb] and thereby [verb] ... · [subject] [auxiliary] thereby [verb] ... · [independent clause]; thereby, [independent clause]. — rare
entries.punctuation: A plain comma before it in the ordinary participial pattern, because what follows is a phrase and not an independent clause — The city rezoned the block, thereby allowing apartments must not take a semicolon. In the rare case where a full independent clause does follow, the semicolon-or-period rule that governs therefore and consequently applies, and a comma alone would be a comma splice. No comma after it in any pattern.
entries.variants: hereby (performative, not result), whereby (hangs on a noun)
entries.see also: whereby, thus, hence, therefore, as a result

entries.meaning: Draws a conclusion from what came before, and is strongest in argument, proof, and formal decisions. It is not a coordinating conjunction, and treating it as one is the single most common punctuation error in American student writing. In speech, people simply say so.
examples: The signature was forged; therefore, the contract is void.
All three witnesses contradicted each other. Therefore, the jury acquitted.
The tests came back clean; the recall was therefore lifted on Monday.
She had already left the company and was, therefore, not on the call.
Therefore, we recommend rejecting the bid in its current form.
Costs rose while revenue stayed flat; therefore, margins narrowed.
entries.русский: поэтому, следовательно — книжн.: вывод; не союз, перед ним нужна точка с запятой
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; therefore, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Therefore, [independent clause]. · [subject] [auxiliary] therefore [verb] ... · [subject] [verb], therefore, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses, and a comma after it at the head of a clause. Mid-clause it takes a comma on each side or none at all, consistently. It rained, therefore we canceled is a comma splice; write It rained; therefore, we canceled.
entries.variants: ergo (jocular or strictly logical)
entries.see also: thus, hence, thereby, consequently, accordingly, as a result, so (coordinating)

entries.meaning: "In this way" and "as a consequence" at once. That double sense is why it can head a participial phrase, a pattern therefore cannot take: The mold was reused, thus cutting costs. It is standard in academic prose and stiff in conversation.
examples: The sensor recalibrates every hour; thus, drift stays under one percent.
Two reviewers dropped out, thus leaving the panel one member short.
The mold was reused, thus cutting production costs nearly in half.
The evidence was obtained without a warrant and was thus excluded at trial.
Thus, the hypothesis cannot be rejected on the present data.
Enrollment fell for a third year — thus the decision to close the campus.
entries.русский: таким образом, тем самым — книжн., науч.: одновременно и способ, и следствие
entries.clause type: independent clause; also modifies a following participle
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; thus, [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Thus, [independent clause]. · [independent clause], thus [-ing participle phrase]. · [independent clause] — thus [noun phrase]. — verbless tag · [subject] [auxiliary] thus [verb] ...
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses, and the comma after it is optional. Before an -ing participle (thus leaving the panel short) a plain comma is correct, because no second independent clause follows, and the same goes for the verbless tag (thus the decision to close the campus), which takes a comma or a dash.
entries.variants: thusly is nonstandard; avoid it
entries.see also: therefore, hence, thereby, consequently, accordingly
